clue.text: Annual arrival of imposing appearance

definitions.meaning: the month that turns up once every year, the eighth of the calendar
majestic, venerable and dignified in bearing

explanation.surface: Something grand and impressive that shows up once a year.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the calendar month that comes round yearly; the other is the adjective meaning majestic or awe-inspiring.

clue.text: A 5d. rise can appear expedient

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece rises, reading upwards, so it is turned round

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five and d. the old abbreviation for a penny, so 5d. gives V then D
can means is able

explanation.surface: A fivepenny price rise may seem sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: '5d.' reads as fivepence in old British money, but it splits into V (five) and D (penny), which 'rise' turns to DV.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a course that is wise or prudent in the circumstances.

clue.text: Leave to play in Hants

parts.note: to go is to leave
to sport is to play or frolic

explanation.surface: Being allowed time off for games in Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Hants is the abbreviation for Hampshire, an English south-coast county, where this naval town stands.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a naval town on Portsmouth Harbour in Hampshire.

clue.text: Community payment

definitions.meaning: a village or colony of people living together
the paying off of a debt or account

explanation.surface: Money paid to a local community.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a newly founded colony or village, and also the discharge of a bill.

clue.text: Neat and direct

definitions.meaning: of a drink, undiluted, with no mixer added
going in a line without bends or detours

explanation.surface: A description of something tidy and to the point.
explanation.definitionFit: A neat whisky is served undiluted, and a direct route has no turns: both senses are this one adjective.

clue.text: Fair distribution of beer to all

indicators.note: distributing the letters spreads them out into a new order

explanation.surface: Sharing beer out to everyone is only fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of middling, passable or acceptable.

clue.text: What Paul and others did

parts.note: a book of the New Testament records the deeds of Paul, Peter and the other apostles

explanation.surface: A question about the doings of a man named Paul and his friends.
explanation.definitionFit: The book of the Bible after the Gospels tells of the deeds of the apostles, Paul chief among them.

clue.text: Is assumed to be a stick-in-the-mud ?

definitions.text: Is assumed to be a stick-in-the-mud ?

parts.words: Is assumed to be a stick-in-the-mud ?
parts.note: assumed means put on, as clothing is; this rubber footwear is pulled on and then sticks fast in mud

explanation.surface: Someone is presumed to be a dull, old-fashioned person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assumed' here means donned, and the stick-in-the-mud is literal: a wellington stuck in the mire.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber wellington boot is worn, or put on, for wading through mud, where it can get stuck.

clue.text: Calls the, conditions

definitions.meaning: names or describes, as in what one calls something
the stipulations of an agreement

explanation.surface: Someone names the requirements.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means names or designates; as a noun it means the stipulations of a contract.

clue.text: Decline to give up

definitions.meaning: a fall or reduction, as in prices
abandon or stop, as one abandons a plan

explanation.surface: Refusing to surrender.
explanation.definitionFit: A fall in value, and the verb meaning to abandon an idea or a habit.

clue.text: Someone calling for a mask ? That's about it

indicators.note: the mask word goes round the outside of the word it, as 'That's about it' says

parts.note: a visor is a face shield or mask, as on a helmet

explanation.surface: Someone at the door wants a disguise, and that is all there is to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's about it' reads as a shrug, but 'That' points back to the mask word, which goes about IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A caller is a guest who drops in, someone paying a visit.

clue.text: Bishop is to send a pound back

indicators.note: the whole run of pieces is read backwards from its end, as the word back signals here

parts.note: to remit is to send money
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: A bishop is told to return a pound he was given.
explanation.walkthrough: REMIT + A + L gives REMITAL, and 'back' turns the whole run around.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Latimer was an English Protestant bishop burned at Oxford in 1555.

clue.text: Booty left by meddler

parts.note: spoils are plunder or loot taken by victors
port is the left-hand side of a ship

explanation.surface: Plunder abandoned by a busybody.
explanation.definitionFit: A killjoy who interferes to ruin others' fun is the person described as a meddler here.

clue.text: Perhaps the Tom mentioned in Lear ?

definitions.text: Perhaps the Tom mentioned in Lear ?

parts.words: Perhaps the Tom mentioned in Lear ?
parts.note: Lear here is Edward Lear, the nonsense poet, not Shakespeare's king; the Tom is a tomcat, the poet's pet tabby that he wrote and drew about

explanation.surface: Asks whether a Tom is named in King Lear, where 'Poor Tom' does appear.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's King Lear has 'Poor Tom', which is the false trail; the Lear meant is Edward Lear, whose cat was famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear's beloved tabby tomcat bore this name and appears in his drawings and letters.

clue.text: Stupid mistake about haymaker in Bennett's novel

annotationWithheld.why: Stupid mistake about haymaker in Bennett's novel: CLANGER must hold YHA (or AYH), an anagram of HAY, but the only word for it is 'haymaker', so 'maker' would be both part of the fodder word and the anagram indicator
annotationWithheld.clue: Stupid mistake about haymaker in Bennett's novel

clue.text: Better half meets half-back early

indicators.note: half of the word Better is its first three letters
the half word is turned round, read from its end, as back says

parts.note: semi- is the prefix meaning half

explanation.surface: A wife meets a footballer playing half-back early on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better half' looks like the wife and 'half-back' like a footballer; 'meets' only joins BET to IMES, which is SEMI turned back.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for in good time or soon, so it stands for the adverb early.

clue.text: Ships carry the right pennons

indicators.note: the ships word carries the other piece inside it

parts.note: steamers are steam-driven ships

explanation.surface: Vessels fly the correct flags.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrow flags or ribbons flown from a mast are both these and pennons.

clue.text: Hold up troubles non-U members

indicators.note: the remaining letters are put back together as members of a new arrangement
non-U says the letter U is to be left out of the word beside it

explanation.surface: Something that supports people through hard times, though members are not upper-class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-U' is the old phrase for not upper-class, but here it drops U from TROUBLES, leaving TROBLES to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To prop up or support something is to bolster it, as a long pillow supports a sleeper.

clue.text: Recount memories of odd crimes in the east

indicators.note: odd says the letters of crimes in are put into a strange new order

explanation.surface: An old criminal recalls his unusual offences out East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the east' looks like a location, but 'in' is fodder and E is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall past experiences aloud and fondly is to tell of memories.

clue.text: Roe returns to embrace thin girl

indicators.note: the turned-round word goes around the other piece, holding it as in a hug
the word Roe is turned back to front, as returns signals

parts.note: taken as written
lean means thin, without fat

explanation.surface: A man named Roe comes back to hug a slim girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' makes EOR from Roe, and 'to embrace' puts LEAN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, so the clue's girl stands for it.

clue.text: First race-horse having black-out ?

definitions.meaning: the unbeaten eighteenth-century champion racehorse, sire of a great line of thoroughbreds
the darkening of the sun or moon when another body passes in front

explanation.surface: A top horse that suffers a loss of consciousness.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous racehorse of the 1760s gave rise to the saying 'Eclipse first, the rest nowhere'.
explanation.definitionFit: A legendary undefeated racehorse bore the name, and the word also means the blotting out of a heavenly body's light.

clue.text: See a problem about one delightful place

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city whose bishop's see is a common crossword see

indicators.note: the problem word is placed about, around, the other piece

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A visit to sort out a difficulty concerning a lovely spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is a bishop's see, here Ely.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the blessed went after death to these Elysian Fields, a paradise.

clue.text: Meantime, if one leaves it's during school-time

indicators.note: it's links the answer less one to the phrase, so the letter for one sits inside the school-time phrase

parts.note: during school-time is in term, written as one run
I is the Roman numeral for one; this is the letter that leaves the answer

explanation.surface: Meanwhile, if a person goes away, it happens during the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs backwards: if one (I) leaves the answer, it's IN TERM, so 'it's' puts I inside INTERM.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean the time in between, the interval before something else happens.

clue.text: Experienced hat-maker ?

definitions.meaning: sensed or undergone, past tense of feel
the matted fabric from which many hats are made

explanation.surface: A seasoned milliner.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the past tense of feel, and also the cloth that trilbies and fedoras are pressed from.

clue.text: As good and bad employees may be, with enthusiasm

definitions.text: As good and bad employees may be
definitions.meaning: bad workers are sacked, while good ones are filled with zeal
inspired or roused, as when filled with ardour

explanation.surface: Workers both good and bad can be enthusiastic.
explanation.walkthrough: Bad employees get dismissed; good ones are filled with zeal: one word covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: It means dismissed from a job, and also stirred up or inspired, as in filled with ardour.

clue.text: Ulster statesman about to stop in Surrey

indicators.note: the statesman's name goes about, round, the stopping word

parts.note: Edward Carson led Ulster Unionist resistance to Irish Home Rule
to halt is to stop

explanation.surface: A Northern Irish politician is about to make a stop in a southern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to stop' reads as 'on the point of stopping', but 'about' is a container. Surrey is a county south of London, where this suburb lies.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a suburban town in the county of Surrey, now part of the London Borough of Sutton.

clue.text: Part of a serious or tragic kind

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A kind of drama that is partly serious or tragic.
explanation.definitionFit: Kind and type are synonyms, as in 'what kind of person'.

clue.text: Tough work, going through this economist !

definitions.meaning: a grind or hard routine
John Stuart ..., the Victorian philosopher and economist

explanation.surface: Hard labour for someone who studies economics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going through the mill' is the idiom for a hard ordeal; the economist is J S Mill.
explanation.definitionFit: A grinding hard time is 'the mill', and John Stuart Mill wrote Principles of Political Economy.

clue.text: Yearly charge is in force again

definitions.meaning: in old land law, an annual deduction or payment charged on an estate
taken up again or renewed, as in a repeated performance

explanation.surface: An annual fee that has been reinstated.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal sense: an annual sum paid out of an estate; general sense: a repetition or renewal of something.

clue.text: Looks kind, often ?

definitions.meaning: gazes at or watches, as a verb
the word that so often follows kind at the foot of a letter

explanation.surface: Looks that are frequently gentle.
explanation.definitionFit: It means gazes at, and is the greeting often signed off 'kind' something at the end of a letter.

clue.text: One may be still due and needing satisfaction

definitions.text: One may be still due and needing satisfaction

indicators.note: the letters of still due may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone still owed something and seeking redress.
explanation.walkthrough: Demanding satisfaction was the formal challenge to a fight with pistols or swords, so the whole clue describes the answer as well as hiding its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A fighter in a formal combat, the affair of honour fought to obtain satisfaction for an insult.

clue.text: With Greek Miss Woodhouse turns out a lightweight

indicators.note: the heroine's first name is turned round, read from its end

parts.note: Emma Woodhouse is the heroine of Jane Austen's novel Emma

explanation.surface: Jane Austen's heroine, joined by a Greek, proves to be a featherweight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns out' looks like 'proves to be' but turns EMMA into AMME.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the older spelling of the metric unit of mass, a tiny weight.
